newsitem.title: UK: HORSE RACING-UK'S MAJOR, PRINCESS ANNE JOIN CROWDS AT NATIONAL.
newsitem.headline: HORSE RACING-UK'S MAJOR, PRINCESS ANNE JOIN CROWDS AT NATIONAL.

text.p: Prime Minister John Major, vowing the IRA would never bomb the British out of their way of life, on Monday joined 20,000 defiant racegoers to watch the Grand National, resurrected 48 hours after a suspected IRA bomb alert forced its abandonment.
They cheered home the 14-1 shot Lord Gyllene, a spectacular all-the-way winner of the world's most famous steeplechase that had been plunged into chaos on Saturday on its 150th birthday.
The winner was ridden by Tony Dobbin a jockey born in Northern Ireland where almost 3,000 people have been killed in the Irish Republican Army (IRA) battle to oust Britain from the province.
Still on a high after the biggest victory of his career, Dobbin said he wanted the race above all to be remembered for the magnificent performance of the 25-length winner.
Major, the target of an IRA mortar bomb attack on his London residence six years ago, flew in by helicopter to watch the race and offer a blunt message to IRA guerrillas.
"Nobody can bomb Britain out of their national instincts and national habits," he told reporters in the paddock before one of the highlights of the British sporting calendar.

"I think that's a message to the IRA and a clear message to the rest of the world as well," he told reporters on a lightning trip to Aintree racecourse in the middle of the campaign for Britain's May 1 general election.
He confessed to fancying a gamble on the favourite, who eventually finished among the also-rans.
"Well I'm very tempted, given the nature of life, to say Go Ballistic."

Police laid on the tightest security ever seen on a British racecourse for the running of the great race that lay in ruins on Saturday night after the mass evacuation of 70,000 fans from the sprawling Aintree track.
As the election approaches, the IRA has stepped up its campaign of violence in a bid to force Northern Ireland onto the political agenda.
In the last two weeks, the guerrillas have planted bombs on British railways and motorways and disrupted London's train services with hoax calls.
Buckingham Palace also delivered its own clear signal after Saturday's fiasco.
Princess Anne, Queen Elizabeth's horse-loving daughter, returned to enjoy the race which she had to leave so hurriedly on Saturday before it could be run.
Thousands of race fans queued patiently outside the track for their free day out at the races.
Each racegoer had to be individually frisked by security staff. Every bag was meticulously checked. Police helicopters hovered over the track. Even the paddock rails were checked for explosives.

Liverpudlians were in proud and defiant mood after a weekend spent hastily finding thousands of stranded racegoers a meal and a bed for the night after they were marooned in this northwest English city famed as the birthplace of the Beatles.
"It is important to be here to show support for the race and show the IRA that nothing will stop us," said Maria Allen, making her first trip to the famous steeplechase.
As the racing daily The Sporting Life boasted in its own defiant headline -- "The Show goes on."
